narrative:
The model predicted a 57% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Three factors drove this outcome, ranked by importance. Your LSAT score was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. At 25, it sits well below the average of 37 among students who were accepted, signaling weaker preparation in the eyes of the model. Your first-year law school grades came next; being in the bottom decile (compared to an average of 6 among accepted students) added a clear push toward failure. Your third-year grades actually worked in your favor, pulling the prediction slightly back toward passing, but not enough to overcome the other two signals.

Taken together, the low LSAT and weak first-year performance outweighed your upper-middle family background, part-time plans, and later improvement.

What you should do next is straightforward: retake the LSAT and aim for a substantially higher score, then reapply. A stronger LSAT would likely flip the model’s prediction and open the door to admission. Focus your energy there; it is the single change that would most improve your chances. (198 words)
